title: Jobs and the Labor Market
description: Ten calm texts about work: a first job interview, how unemployment is counted, a landscaping apprentice, remote work weighed fairly, a career counselor, a new career at fifty, the history of the weekend, a town after its factory closed, a bakery lab and a rhino sanctuary warden.

lessons.title: The Interview at the Museum
lessons.summary: A young graduate prepares for her first real job interview, at a natural history museum, and gets the job.
lessons.text:
Lena Ortiz was twenty-two, had just finished college, and had never had a real job interview. Her earlier jobs, in a coffee shop and walking dogs, had come through friends. This time she had applied to be a part-time educator at the city's natural history museum, and the museum had invited her to come in on Thursday morning.

For a week, her older brother badgered her to prepare. He badgered her at breakfast and by text message: had she read about the museum, had she practiced her answers? Lena found it tiring, but she prepared. She read the job description until she knew it almost by heart. It said the museum wanted someone who could explain science to children, "preferably with some teaching experience." Lena had none, but she had tutored younger students in math for two years, and she decided to present that honestly. The description also emphasized patience and a friendly manner.

The pay was hourly, and the schedule was irregular: some mornings for school groups, some weekends, and a few evening events. Lena did not mind. Hourly pay was enough for a start, and an irregular schedule would leave her time for evening classes, preferably two a week.

On Thursday she arrived early and met the head of education, a calm woman named Carol Grant, in a small office.

The questions were not what Lena had expected. Carol handed her a dark, heavy stone and asked her to explain it as if she were talking to a class of ten-year-olds. A small card said it was a piece of an asteroid. Lena took a breath. She said that an asteroid is a rocky body that travels around the sun, and that once in a while a small piece falls through the air and lands on Earth. Then she asked the imaginary children to guess why the stone was so heavy: it contained a lot of iron.

Next, Carol showed her a photo of black rock full of small holes. Lena explained that volcanic rock forms when melted rock from deep underground cools at the surface, and that the holes are left by bubbles of gas. Finally, Carol asked how she would keep a group of children interested in the jaguar display. Lena said she would ask them to find the jaguar before she told them anything, because its spotted coat is made for hiding in the forest.

At the end, Lena emphasized two things: she loved explaining things, and she learned quickly. Her brother had said that a good closing statement could clinch a job. She did not know whether hers had, but she left feeling that she had been herself.

Two days later, the museum offered her the job. What had clinched it, Carol told her later, was the way she had asked the children questions instead of simply giving a lecture.

Questions:
What did Lena's brother do during the week before the interview?
He badgered her to prepare, at breakfast and by text message.
What is an asteroid, according to Lena?
An asteroid is a rocky body that travels around the sun.
How does volcanic rock form?
It forms when melted rock from deep underground cools at the surface.
What clinched the job for Lena?
The way she asked the children questions instead of simply giving a lecture clinched it.

lessons.title: How Unemployment Is Counted
lessons.summary: A short report explains how the unemployment rate is measured and why one number cannot tell the whole story.
lessons.text:
Every month, the news reports a single number: the unemployment rate. It looks simple, but behind it lies a careful method worth knowing.

In the United States, the figure comes from a monthly survey of about 60,000 households. Trained staff ask people what they did during one particular week. A person counts as employed if he or she did any paid work that week, even a few hours. A person counts as unemployed only if three things are true: they had no job, they were available to work, and they had actively looked for work during the past four weeks. Everyone else, such as students, retired people and parents caring for children at home, is outside the labor force and does not appear in the rate at all.

This definition gives a simplified picture of real life, and a simplified picture always leaves something out. Imagine a woman who wants a job but has stopped looking because she believes nothing is available in her town. Because she has not searched in the past four weeks, she is not counted as unemployed. Economists describe her attachment to the labor force as marginal: she sits at the edge, not searching now but ready to return if a chance appeared. The government therefore also publishes a broader measure that includes these marginal workers.

Contingent workers are people whose jobs are not expected to last, such as temporary staff. A contingent worker may be employed this month and searching the next, so the official rate can look healthier than many households feel.

Changes in the rate also need care. A falling rate usually signifies good news, but not always. If many people give up searching, the rate can move downward even though nobody has found work. On the other hand, the rate sometimes rises early in a recovery, when people who had given up start looking again. In that case a rise may signify hope rather than trouble.

Economists therefore compare each new figure with a baseline, often the average of the previous few years, before they judge how serious a change is. After a recession, job losses usually taper slowly over many months, and if the recovery slows, hiring may taper off as well.

Not everyone who leaves a job is a victim of hard times. Many people quit voluntarily, to move, to study or to take a better offer. When large numbers of workers leave voluntarily, it usually signifies confidence in the job market.

Finally, unemployment touches people indirectly. When a parent loses work, the children feel it, and so do the local shops. No number can show how many lives are affected indirectly, which is why the rate is best read as a starting point, not a final answer.

Questions:
Who counts as unemployed in the survey?
A person who had no job, was available to work, and had looked for work during the past four weeks.
Why is the woman who stopped looking not counted as unemployed?
She has not searched in the past four weeks, so her attachment to the labor force is only marginal.
Can a falling rate signify bad news?
Yes. The rate can move downward when people give up searching, even though nobody has found work.
What do economists compare a new figure with?
They compare it with a baseline, often the average of the previous few years.

lessons.title: The Apprentice at the Lake House
lessons.summary: A first-year landscaping apprentice learns about stone, water and safety while working with his teacher at a house by a lake.
lessons.text:
Marcus Hill was 19 and in the first year of an apprenticeship in landscape work. His program was accredited by the state, which meant that its hours and lessons met an official standard. He worked four days a week for Ray Delgado, who built gardens, paths and walls, and spent the fifth day in class at the community college. At the end of the accredited program, he would receive a certificate that employers across the state would recognize.

One spring morning, Ray and Marcus drove to a house by a lake, where the owner, an old man named Mr. Lund, wanted a new garden path and a repaired pond. Their first job was to unload the truck. Ray showed Marcus how to unload heavy bags properly: knees bent, back straight, the weight close to the body. Then they unloaded two tons of gravel for the path. Later they spread the gravel and pressed it down until it was firm and even.

Before any work had begun, Ray had written the owner a quotation, and he had shown Marcus how a quotation is made: you measure the area, list every material, estimate the hours and add a little for surprises. "A good quotation is honest," he said. "If it is too low, you lose money. If it is too high, you lose the customer."

Mr. Lund had one idea of his own. He wanted a low wall built from the gray stone on the hill behind the house. Ray picked up a piece, and it split into thin layers in his hand. It was shale, he explained, a soft rock made from ancient mud. Shale breaks apart in rain and frost, so a wall of shale would not last. They agreed to use harder stone for the wall.

Cutting the hard stone was serious work. The saw threw up fine dust, which can harm the lungs over time, so the saw ran with water to keep the dust down, and both men wore masks. The saw's water hose did not fit Mr. Lund's garden hose, so Marcus fetched an adapter from the truck. Ray always carried a box of adapters for exactly this reason.

The pond came last. Its surface was covered with green scum, a thin layer of tiny plants that grows quickly in still, sunny water. To keep the scum from coming back, they added a small pump to move the water and planted tall plants along one side, so that part of the pond would stay shady. Cool, moving water in a shady pond is much less friendly to scum.

At lunch they sat on the dock. A large brown and white bird dove into the lake and rose with a fish. "A seahawk," said Mr. Lund. Ray told Marcus that most people call it an osprey, but the old name, seahawk, is still common by the water.

Questions:
What does it mean that Marcus's program was accredited?
It means that its hours and lessons met an official standard.
What makes a good quotation, according to Ray?
A good quotation is honest, neither too low nor too high.
Why did they not build the wall from shale?
Shale is a soft rock that breaks apart in rain and frost, so the wall would not last.
How did they keep the scum from coming back?
They added a pump to move the water and planted tall plants to make part of the pond shady.

lessons.title: Working from Home, Weighed Calmly
lessons.summary: A columnist who has worked both at home and in an office weighs the good and bad sides of remote work.
lessons.text:
A few years ago, working from home went from rare to normal almost overnight. For a while it was the height of vogue: magazines photographed home offices, and companies promised that the old office was gone for good. Then some employers began calling people back. Today remote work is unpopular with many managers, while the return to the office is just as unpopular with many workers. Having done both, I would like to weigh them calmly.

Start with time. When I worked downtown, my day seemed to revolve around the train: when it left, whether it was late, how crowded it would be. Now my day revolves around my work and my family, and I have gained more than an hour each day. For parents, gaining that hour is akin to a small promotion, paid in time rather than money.

Home also offers ample room to concentrate. In an open office I was interrupted all day; at my kitchen table I can write for two hours without a single question. There is ample evidence that work which needs deep focus goes better in quiet surroundings.

Yet the other side deserves a fair hearing. The line between work and relaxation becomes thin when your office is also your living room. On bad days I check my email at nine in the evening, and real relaxation never quite arrives. It is easy to dwell on a small problem when nobody at the next desk can laugh it off with you. A friend of mine once dwelt on one sharp email for a whole afternoon.

Younger workers may lose the most. Much of what I learned in my first job I learned by listening to experienced people on the phone, which is akin to an apprenticeship that nobody plans. On a video call, that kind of learning rarely happens.

I have learned to disable notifications after six o'clock, and I would advise anyone to disable them too. On the other hand, some companies misuse the tools that make remote work possible, for example by recording how often staff move their computer mouse. Such misuse destroys trust quickly.

The answer, I suspect, is neither the old office nor the kitchen table but a redesign of the working week. The current vogue is a mixed week: staff come in on two or three days for meetings, training and the simple pleasure of company, and stay home for focused work. Some firms have gone further, with a redesign of the office itself: fewer rows of desks and more rooms for talking.

No single pattern will suit everyone. A young person in a shared apartment and a parent with a quiet study have different needs. Good employers, it seems to me, will ask before they decide.

Questions:
What did the writer's day revolve around in the downtown job?
It revolved around the train: when it left, whether it was late and how crowded it was.
Why does home offer ample room to concentrate?
At home nobody interrupts, so the writer can write for two hours without a single question.
What problem does the writer have with relaxation?
When the office is also the living room, the writer cannot switch off, and real relaxation never quite arrives.
What does the writer advise people to disable?
The writer advises them to disable notifications after six o'clock.
What redesign of the working week does the writer describe?
Staff come in on two or three days for meetings and training and stay home for focused work.

lessons.title: The Counselor Who Listens First
lessons.summary: A profile of a community college career counselor and the patient way she helps people find work.
lessons.text:
Ruth Okafor has been a career counselor at a community college in Ohio for twenty-four years. On most days she sees six or seven people in her small office. Some are students choosing a first career. Others are adults who have lost a job and arrive, as Ruth puts it, "in a funk": tired, discouraged, and unsure where to begin.

Ruth does not try to be a savior. "People expect me to hand them the perfect job," she says, "but I am not anyone's savior. My work is to help people see what they already have." She begins every meeting the same way, by asking people to describe a day when work went well. Most visitors are surprised. They came to talk about what went wrong, and she wants to hear what went right.

Her method is to nurture confidence before she talks about resumes. She believes that people who feel useless cannot sell themselves, so she spends the first meetings helping them name their skills. A woman who managed a busy restaurant kitchen, for example, may not see that she can also organize people and solve problems under pressure. Once that confidence has been nurtured, the practical work begins.

Ruth also confers regularly with local employers, from hospitals to factories, to learn which skills they need. When she has conferred with enough of them, she can tell a student which courses are worth the time and money. The work requires diplomacy. Employers sometimes complain that young people are not ready for work, and students complain that employers expect too much. Ruth listens to both with the same diplomacy and tries to bring them together.

She is careful not to aggravate people's fears. Many visitors have read that machines will soon take every job, a kind of jobs apocalypse. Ruth answers calmly. Technology has always changed work, she says, and the jobs apocalypse that people predicted many times in the past never arrived. Some jobs did disappear, but new ones appeared. Telling a frightened person that the future is dark would only aggravate the fear, so she prefers to talk about the next step.

She also warns against a certain idea of greatness. "Young people think they must find their passion and achieve greatness by the age of twenty-five," she says. "But most careers are built slowly, one decision at a time. Greatness, if it comes, usually comes later." Last year she put her advice into a short ebook for students, which the college gives away for free. A former student reblogged a page from the ebook, others reblogged it in turn, and now readers from other states sometimes write to Ruth. She is pleased, but what she values most is still the quiet conversation in her small office.

Questions:
How do many adults feel when they first visit Ruth?
They arrive in a funk: tired, discouraged and unsure where to begin.
Why does Ruth say she is not anyone's savior?
She says her work is to help people see what they already have.
What does Ruth nurture before she talks about resumes?
She nurtures confidence, helping people name their skills.
Why does Ruth confer with local employers?
She confers with them to learn which skills they need.
How does Ruth answer people who fear a jobs apocalypse?
She says that technology has always changed work and that the apocalypse predicted in the past never arrived.

lessons.title: Starting Over at Fifty
lessons.summary: An office manager leaves his career at fifty, buys a small orchard and learns to farm.
lessons.text:
For twenty-six years, Tom Becker worked in an insurance office, where he managed a team that handled claims. He was good at it and well paid. But at forty-nine he realized that he spent his weekends waiting for something to begin. His happiest days, he noticed, were the ones he spent working in his sister's garden.

The year he turned fifty, Tom made a decision that surprised his colleagues: he bought a small orchard in the hills two hours from the city. It had four hundred apple trees and an old barn. He did not pay for it all at once. He and the former owner, a retired farmer named Walter Price, agreed that Tom would pay a large first installment and the rest in yearly installments over ten years. In return, Walter promised to teach him the work.

The first lessons were humbling. Tom had managed people, but he had never driven a tractor. In the spring, Walter showed him how to plow the strip of land where they would plant young trees. Tom plowed a crooked line on the first day and a straight one by the end of the week. Walter told him that every new farmer starts with crooked lines.

The orchard also had a field of grass, which they cut in early summer and rolled into large round bales. Tom sold most of the bales to a neighbor who kept horses and used a few to protect the young trees from the wind. Along the fence grew wild blackberry bushes. Walter advised him to keep them, because bees visit blackberry flowers and then help the apple trees as well.

Money was a worry. In his first year, Tom earned less than a third of his old salary, and he had to learn things that no office had taught him, such as how a frost in May can ruin a whole crop. He kept careful records, the one office skill that farming needed every day.

In September the apples were ready, large, sweet and juicy. Tom opened the orchard to families who wanted to pick their own fruit, and on the first Saturday a long caravan of cars came slowly up the hill road from the city. By the end of the season, these caravans of visitors had become the most profitable part of the business. Children ran between the rows with juicy apples they had picked themselves.

Not every apple was perfect. Fruit with small marks went to the local food bank, which became the main beneficiary of the apples that nobody wanted to buy. Tom was glad that hungry families, rather than the trash, were the beneficiary.

He does not tell everyone to leave their job at fifty. Farming is hard work, and it pays less. But when friends ask whether he regrets it, he says he no longer waits for the weekend.

Questions:
How did Tom pay for the orchard?
He paid a large first installment and the rest in yearly installments over ten years.
What did Walter teach Tom in the spring?
He showed him how to plow the land where they would plant young trees.
Why did Walter advise Tom to keep the blackberry bushes?
Bees visit the blackberry flowers and then help the apple trees as well.
Who was the beneficiary of the apples with small marks?
The local food bank was the main beneficiary.

lessons.title: How We Got the Weekend
lessons.summary: A short history of the weekend, from medieval holy days to the five-day week.
lessons.text:
Most of us take the weekend for granted, yet it was built slowly, over many centuries, by religion, custom and law.

In medieval England, a peasant family farmed its own small fields but also had to work on the fields of the local lord. The work was organized by the reeve, a peasant chosen to decide who would plow or cut hay on a given day, count the harvest and report to the lord. The peasants lived under the lord's dominion, and the king could demand their money too: when King Richard was captured abroad in 1192, ordinary people across England had to help pay the huge ransom for his release through a heavy tax.

There was, however, one limit on the lord's dominion: the church. Since 321 AD, when the Roman emperor Constantine declared Sunday a day of rest, Sunday had been set apart for worship. In the eyes of the church, a person who worked on Sunday without need was a sinner. The fear of being seen as a sinner gave ordinary people one free day, and the holy days of the year gave them more.

Later, the state added its own rules. Under the English monarchy, a law of 1677 made it unlawful to work at ordinary trades or sell goods on Sunday. In parts of the United States, too, it remained unlawful to open certain shops on Sunday until quite recently. The monarchy and the church protected a day of rest, though their reason was worship, not leisure.

Around 1800, many English workers in small trades also took Monday off, a custom they called Saint Monday. The custom is now a relic of the past, and few people know its name, but it shows that workers wanted more free time long before the law gave it to them. As factories grew, employers disliked the custom, and a compromise appeared: a free Saturday afternoon in exchange for a full Monday.

In Britain, Parliament began to legalize trade unions in 1871, and once unions had been legalized, they could bargain openly for shorter hours. In the United States, Henry Ford gave his factory workers a five-day week in 1926, arguing that people with free time would buy more goods. When Saturday became a free day, families trooped to parks, beaches and ball games, and shoppers trooped into the stores.

In 1938, a law in the United States set a standard working week, which reached forty hours by 1940. Since then the two-day weekend has become normal in much of the world, although nurses, shop staff and many others still work on weekends.

The Sunday shopping laws that survive in some places are a remnant of the old religious rules, and the word holiday itself is a remnant of the holy day. For a medieval peasant, two free days a week would have seemed worth a king's ransom, an old phrase for an enormous sum.

Questions:
What did the reeve do in medieval England?
The reeve organized the work on the lord's fields, counted the harvest and reported to the lord.
Why was a person who worked on Sunday called a sinner?
In the eyes of the church, Sunday was set apart for worship, so working without need was wrong.
What did the law of 1677 make unlawful?
It made it unlawful to work at ordinary trades or sell goods on Sunday.
What is Saint Monday?
It was a custom of English workers who took Monday off, and it is now a relic of the past.

lessons.title: The Town That Built Again
lessons.summary: After its engine-parts factory closed, a small town slowly found new work, though not every problem was solved.
lessons.text:
For seventy years, the town of Millbrook lived by its factory. The plant on the river made pistons for car and truck engines, millions of them, and at its busiest it employed nearly two thousand people. A piston is the metal part that moves up and down inside an engine, and in Millbrook almost every family knew someone who had made, tested or packed them.

In 2009, the company decided to move production elsewhere, and the plant was shuttered. Within a year, the shuttered building had become a symbol of the town's trouble. Nearly two thousand jobs had vanished, and so had many of the businesses that depended on them, from a hardware store to two clothing shops. When the jobs vanished, some families moved away, and the high school lost a third of its students.

For a few years, the mood was close to hopeless. Yet not everyone felt hopeless, and some people began to meet in the library to discuss what might come next.

The company put the empty factory up for sale. Several bidders looked at the site, and the highest bidder planned to tear it down for a warehouse that would employ only a few dozen people. Instead, the town council supported an offer from a consortium: the community college, a local bank, the county, and three small companies. The consortium paid less than the highest bidder, but it promised to keep the building and divide it into spaces for many smaller employers.

The changes came slowly. The college opened a training center in the east wing, where people learn nursing, machine and computer skills. A young company that makes carbon nanotubes moved into the west wing. A nanotube is a tiny tube of carbon, thousands of times thinner than a human hair, yet very strong, and the company sells nanotubes to firms that make batteries and light materials. It hired several former factory workers, whose skill with precise machines was just what it needed.

Smaller things mattered too. A woman who had worked in the factory office for twenty years opened a pottery studio in the old loading area, and her pottery classes are now full every evening. In the park by the river, volunteers built a wooden pavilion, where a farmers market is held every Saturday. On summer evenings, bands play in the pavilion.

The story is still unfinished. The new jobs number only about half of the old ones, and many pay less. Some older workers never found work again and retired early. The south wing of the old factory is still empty, an unfinished part of the plan. But the town is no longer defined by a single employer, and most people in Millbrook say that is a strength.

Questions:
What did the factory in Millbrook make?
It made pistons, the metal parts that move up and down inside an engine.
What happened after the plant was shuttered?
Nearly two thousand jobs vanished, and many businesses that depended on them closed.
Why did the town support the consortium instead of the highest bidder?
The consortium promised to keep the building and divide it into spaces for many smaller employers.
What is a nanotube?
It is a tiny, very strong tube of carbon, thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
Why is the story still unfinished?
The new jobs are only about half of the old ones, many pay less, and the south wing is still empty.

lessons.title: A Day in the Bakery Lab
lessons.summary: A quality technician at a large bakery spends a day testing flour and bread, and helps replace one ingredient.
lessons.text:
Jenna Park works as a quality technician at a large regional bakery that produces about two hundred thousand loaves of bread a day. Many people imagine bakery work as shaping dough by hand, but Jenna spends most of her day in a small laboratory at the edge of the factory floor, making sure that every loaf is safe and every batch is the same.

Her day begins at six with the flour. Each truck that arrives brings a certificate from the mill, but Jenna still tests samples herself. One test looks for chemical residue, the small amount of a farm spray that can remain on grain after harvest. The law sets a limit for each residue, and the bakery's own limit is stricter. Another test looks for a toxin produced by a mold that sometimes grows on wheat in wet summers. The toxin is invisible and has no smell, so the only way to find it is in the lab. If a sample shows an abnormal level of the toxin, the whole delivery is sent back to the mill.

At nine, Jenna bakes test loaves in a small oven. She weighs everything exactly: the flour, the water, and a level tablespoon of salt for each test batch. A tablespoon more or less would change the taste and the way the dough rises, so she uses the same measuring spoon every time. Then she measures the height of each loaf and cuts it open to examine the crumb, the soft inside of the bread. Large holes or a heavy texture would be abnormal and would tell her that something in the flour or the process has changed.

Part of her job is safety for the workers as well. Fine flour dust can be hazardous to breathe over many years, so she checks the air filters, and she makes sure that the strong cleaning products, which are hazardous to the skin, are stored and labeled correctly.

This year, Jenna also led a special project. For a long time, the bakery had added a small amount of azodicarbonamide to its dough. Azodicarbonamide strengthens dough and makes bread soft and white. It is permitted in small amounts in the United States, but it is not allowed in the countries of the European Union, and some customers had written to ask why the bakery used it. The company decided to remove it. Jenna spent three months testing other ingredients, until she found a recipe that gave the same soft loaf without azodicarbonamide.

She enjoys the work because it combines science with something everyone understands. "Every morning, thousands of families make sandwiches from our bread," she says. "They never think about me, and that is how it should be."

Questions:
What does Jenna look for when she tests the flour?
She looks for chemical residue from farm sprays and for a toxin produced by a mold.
What happens if a sample shows an abnormal level of the toxin?
The whole delivery is sent back to the mill.
Why does Jenna measure a level tablespoon of salt?
A tablespoon more or less would change the taste and the way the dough rises.
Why does she check the air filters?
Fine flour dust can be hazardous to breathe over many years.
Why did the bakery stop using azodicarbonamide?
Customers had asked why it was used, and it is not allowed in the European Union.

lessons.title: The Warden of the Rhinos
lessons.summary: A profile of a sanctuary warden in Kenya who protects rhinos and works closely with the people who live nearby.
lessons.text:
Daniel Kariuki is the senior warden of a rhino sanctuary in northern Kenya. As warden, he is responsible for everything inside its fences: the animals, the land, the roads, the water and about sixty staff. He says that the job is one part science, one part business and three parts talking to people.

The sanctuary protects black rhinos, which were hunted almost to extinction for their horns between 1970 and 1990. Each rhino carries a small tracking device, and every morning teams of scouts walk out to find the animals and record their condition. Many of these scouts are unarmed. They are young men and women from nearby villages who know the land well, and their work is to watch, count and report. The armed rangers, who are trained separately, respond only when there is a threat. Daniel believes that unarmed scouts from the villages do as much to protect the rhinos as any weapon, because they are the eyes of the community.

This year has brought a long drought. Daniel measures its severity by the water holes, the grass and the condition of the animals. When the severity of a drought grows, the sanctuary trucks in water and extra food, and the warden must decide where the money will come from.

The sanctuary also raises orphans. In the spring, keepers found a three-week-old rhino calf alone near a dry river after its mother had died. The calf now lives in a small enclosure and drinks milk from a bottle every three hours, day and night. Visitors often ask to cuddle the calf, and the keepers explain that only they may touch it. Still, on cold nights one young keeper sits beside the calf and lets it cuddle against him, because an orphan needs warmth and company as much as milk.

Not all of the warden's problems involve animals. A few years ago, a malicious rumor spread that the sanctuary planned to take land from the families who keep cattle nearby. The rumor was false, but it was malicious enough to make people angry. Daniel visited each village, sat with the elders and explained the plans in detail. He also offered jobs and school visits, and today about half of the staff come from those villages.

The school visits are his favorite part of the job. Last month, a class of eight-year-olds spent a morning at the sanctuary, watched the orphan calf and asked questions for an hour. At the end, a small girl held out her notebook and asked for his autograph. Daniel laughed and said he was not famous, but he signed it anyway. Several other children then wanted an autograph too. He hopes that some of them will one day become scouts, keepers or even the next warden.

Questions:
What is Daniel responsible for as warden?
He is responsible for the animals, the land, the roads, the water and about sixty staff.
What do the unarmed scouts do?
They walk out to find the rhinos, and they watch, count and report.
How does Daniel measure the severity of the drought?
He measures it by the water holes, the grass and the condition of the animals.
Why does the young keeper let the calf cuddle against him?
An orphan needs warmth and company as much as milk.
How did Daniel answer the malicious rumor?
He visited each village, sat with the elders and explained the plans in detail.
